source.title: Parallel Layer Normalization for Universal Approximation
source.authors: Yun-Hao Ni; Yu-He Liu; Wen-Xin Sun; Yi-Tong Tang; Yu-Xin Guo; Pei-Lin Feng; Wen-Jun Wu; Lei Huang

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present, including appendices. No obvious truncation or garbling that prevents extracting the relevant results.
record.tranche_reason: The paper varies normalization domains and measures fitting accuracy on fixed random labels in a CIFAR-10 CNN, directly testing whether gradient-trained networks fit those labels.
record.gate_note: The paper also reports ViT random-label fitting and a VGG-16 initialization sweep, but those results do not directly measure the CIFAR-10/100 CNN training-error claim in V1. The ViT results are outside V1's CNN setting; the VGG sweep reports test accuracy, not training classification error. The random-label results cited from Zhang et al. are prior work, not rows.
record.test_reason: The study uses the original random-label fitting method and training-classification measure: a randomly initialized CIFAR-10 CNN is trained with SGD, and accuracy on its fixed training labels is measured. Normalization domains vary within one architecture.
record.authors_conclusion: The record accurately summarizes the empirical conclusions but omits the main theoretical conclusion: parallel fixed-dimensional LN units enable universal approximation as their number grows, whereas widening a single shallow LN unit does not. The authors find that finite CNN and ViT performance depends on grouping axes, replacement site, and label structure, and explicitly distinguish finite-model evidence from proof of universality.
record.recipe_differences: Gradient training on CIFAR-10 random labels is tested, but the paper focuses on normalization-domain comparisons in one CNN architecture; it does not test the full range of sizes, optimizers, or recipes in V1.
record.method_sensitivity: Normalization domain and grouping axes change random-label fitting accuracy.

fits_no_version.finding: The VGG-16 initialization and learning-rate sweep reports that PLN[8] is comparatively insensitive to initialization scale, using final three-seed test accuracy.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Final held-out performance of VGG-16 depends on activation, initialization scale, and learning rate; PLN[8] is comparatively robust in this grid.

fits_no_version.finding: ViT random-label fitting depends on token–channel grouping and replacement site.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Grouped normalization can improve finite-sample random-label fitting in the tested ViTs.

fits_no_version.finding: Representation theorems, MLP regression, and PINN experiments concern approximation capacity or solution accuracy.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Parallel fixed-dimensional normalization blocks support universal approximation and useful finite-model approximation performance.

record.problems: The directly relevant CNN comparison is a single depth-4, width-128 architecture on CIFAR-10. Table 2 reports three-seed means without a stated error bar. The paper does not report CIFAR-100 results.
record.rows_left_out: No relevant results left out. The mixed-axis CNN grid in Appendix D.2.1 and ViT results in Section 6.2 and Appendix D.3 are outside the specific CNN conditions recorded here; VGG-16 Figure A3 reports test accuracy rather than training classification error.

untested.parts: CIFAR-100, Adam training of CNNs, systematic model-size thresholds, early stopping, and comparisons across regularization recipes or training durations.
ReLU teacher-student optimization, spurious local minima, and extra student neurons.
Training-error degradation across CNN depths and its prevention by identity shortcuts or special initialization.
Learning speed, trainable depth, signal and gradient propagation, and orthogonal versus Gaussian initialization. The VGG-16 sweep reports final test accuracy.
Initial stability thresholds, loss transients, curvature trajectories, and edge-of-stability behavior.
Matched batch-normalization comparisons of training speed and learning-rate tolerance, and Fixup comparisons.

missing.what: PLN[4] also achieves 100.0% three-seed mean fitting accuracy on the same 50,000 random-label CNN task; Table 2's additional complete-fitting result has no row.

record.verdict_notes: The study is not an original source for these versions. The mixed-axis CNN and clean-label grids are explicitly declared in rows_left_out, so they are not listed as undeclared missing results. The CNN comparisons change the nonlinear function class as well as normalization geometry; they do not isolate optimization failure from representational limitations.

versions.untested_parts: CIFAR-100; Adam; smaller models, early stopping, and regularized recipes; broader model-size and training-duration conditions.

rows.subject: depth-4, width-128 CNN with PLN[8]
rows.operation_detail: Trained on fixed random labels and measured fitting accuracy.
rows.note: Paper says the architecture's grouped normalization replaces every nonlinear layer.
rows.check: Value and subject are correct. Appendix D.2.1 specifies 200 epochs of SGD, learning rate 0.01, momentum 0.9, batch size 128, zero weight decay, and disabled normalization affine parameters. Normalization supplies the nonlinearity; there is no separate element-wise activation.

rows.subject: depth-4, width-128 CNN with Best GN
rows.operation_detail: Trained on fixed random labels and measured fitting accuracy.
rows.note: The paper identifies this as conventional GN using the full spatial map.
rows.check: The 95.8% fitting accuracy means 4.2% training error. Best GN is the selected best conventional-GN configuration, with domain 2×32×32, rather than a separate normalization method. The same training protocol as R1 applies.

source_check.locator_found: Section 6.2, Table 2: Best GN, domain 2×32×32; Appendix D.2.1.

rows.subject: depth-4, width-128 CNN with LN
rows.operation_detail: Trained on fixed random labels and measured fitting accuracy.
rows.note: This is a comparison under the same CNN architecture.
rows.check: The 24.6% fitting accuracy means 75.4% training error, so near-zero training error is absent. LN normalizes the entire 128×32×32 feature map and supplies the only intermediate nonlinearity. The same training protocol as R1 applies.

source_check.locator_found: Section 6.2, Table 2: LN, domain 128×32×32; Appendix D.2.1.
